text.en: In the 1960s India faced food shortages. High-yielding wheat and rice changed that. This is the story of the Green Revolution and the science behind crop improvement.

Crop improvement is developing varieties with higher yield, better quality, resistance to diseases and pests, and shorter duration.
Norman Borlaug developed semi-dwarf wheat and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970; in India M. S. Swaminathan led the Green Revolution.
Semi-dwarf wheat such as Sonalika and Kalyan Sona, and the semi-dwarf rice IR-8, gave high yields because of a dwarfing gene.
Introduction means bringing a variety from another place, and selection chooses the best plants: mass selection is simple and suits inexperienced farmers, pureline selection uses the progeny of a single plant, and clonal selection uses vegetatively propagated plants.
Polyploidy raises the chromosome sets; colchicine doubles chromosomes and gives larger, vigorous plants.
Mutation breeding uses gamma rays or chemicals; the gamma garden produces useful mutants such as salt tolerant rice.
Hybridization crosses two genetically different plants to combine desirable characters, for example the man-made cereal triticale from wheat and rye.
Disease resistant varieties include Pusa Komal in cowpea and Himgiri in wheat; biofortification breeds crops rich in vitamins, minerals and proteins to fight hidden hunger.

problem.en: Which method of crop improvement can an inexperienced farmer practise, and why?

text.en: Mass selection picks plants with the best traits from a mixed population.

why.en: Seeds are then mixed and sown.

text.en: It needs no special crossing skill.
So mass selection suits an inexperienced farmer.
